messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo’s life changed on a Tuesday evening nine months ago. He was walking to his car after his shift when a dark sedan pulled up beside him. Two men in plain clothes but with the unmistakable bearing of authority told him to get in. What followed was forty-eight hours of interrogation and beatings in a windowless room, a nightmare of powerlessness and pain that ended as abruptly as it began when he was pushed out of the same car onto a deserted road. He never found out why he was taken or by whom. The not knowing is a terror of its own, a blank space his mind fills with the worst possible answers.

In the months that followed, the world outside his small apartment began to feel like a minefield. The constant feeling of being hunted settled deep in his bones. He feels threatened by strangers who walk too quickly behind him on the street, his body tensing for an attack that never comes. At his job cleaning offices downtown, a friendly pat on the back from a coworker can make him flinch so violently he has to brace himself against a wall, his heart hammering against his ribs. The sense of danger is so pervasive that sleep offers no respite; he often jolts awake in the middle of the night, his first conscious thought a surge of panic as he strains to hear for footsteps outside his door, absolutely certain he is not safe.

This ever-present sense of threat has reshaped his life into a series of elaborate detours and avoidances. Because his mind is already primed for attack, any person in uniform has become a symbol of profound danger. He now takes a much longer route to work just to avoid passing the local police station. At the office building, he actively avoids his supervisor, whose company-issued polo shirt feels too much like a uniform, a decision that has started to cause friction with management. This hypervigilance also makes him acutely sensitive to new triggers; the sound of any car slowing down on his street is no longer just a noise but a potential threat, a sign that they have come back for him.

The triggers themselves are everywhere, each one sending a fresh wave of panic through him and pushing him deeper into his defensive crouch. Seeing a dark sedan, even one parked across the street, can flood his body with the same cold dread he felt that first night, a certainty that he is being watched. This overwhelming feeling of immediate danger compels him to act; he will duck into an alley, change his direction, or light a cigarette with trembling hands just to have something to do. He has learned to turn off the news instantly if a story involves police or conflict, and he has asked his family not to bring it up. Even moments of happiness feel dangerous; a laugh shared with a friend can be instantly extinguished by a wave of terror, as if feeling good is a luxury he can no longer afford, a vulnerability that will invite disaster.

His strategies for survival have become a cage. The pack-a-day smoking habit he’s developed to manage the anxiety only leaves his nerves more frayed, which his mind interprets as further proof that the world is an unsafe place. His strict refusal to talk about what happened, his strategy for avoiding reminders, was a major factor in his divorce; his ex-wife couldn’t understand why he would shut down and leave the room whenever she tried to offer comfort. This self-imposed isolation has only amplified his sense of being alone and unsafe. The more he avoids, the more his belief that people in authority are dangerous is confirmed, tightening the coil of fear around his daily life and making any accidental encounter with a trigger feel more shocking and potent.

Mateo finally sought help after his supervisor warned him that his avoidance was being interpreted as insubordination. The thought of losing his job, the one remaining piece of structure in his life, was terrifying. He sits in the waiting room, convinced that talking about the trauma will only make it real again, but a small, desperate part of him hopes there is a way to stop checking the locks, to walk down the street without feeling like prey, and to simply feel safe in his own skin again.
